question.text: The diameter of a cylinder is measured using a vernier calipers with no zero error. It is found that the zero of the vernier scale lies between <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>5</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>10</mn><mo> </mo><mi>cm</mi></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>5</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>15</mn><mo> </mo><mi>cm</mi></math> of the main scale. The vernier scale has <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>50</mn></math>  divisions equivalent to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>2</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>45</mn><mo> </mo><mi>cm</mi></math>. The <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mn>24</mn><mi>th</mi></msup></math> division of the vernier scale exactly coincides with one of the main scale divisions. The diameter of the cylinder is,

solution.text:
1 MSD = 0.05 ​
1 VSD = 2.45 5 0 = 0.04
Diameter of the cylinder  
= MSR + L.C. × 2 4
= 5.124 cm
